nodes.label: Genghis Khan destroys Khwarazm
nodes.full: Chinggis Khan's destruction of the Khwarazmian empire in 1219-21 sends the shock west: stateless Khwarazmian cavalry become a wrecking force for hire, and scholars flee toward Ayyubid Syria and Egypt years before the Mongols themselves arrive.
nodes.src: background — see the caliphate-945-1258 folio; Jackson (2017)

nodes.label: Almohad persecution in the Islamic West
nodes.full: The Almohad regime's forced-conversion campaigns in Spain and the Maghrib drive Jewish and Muslim scholars east, among them the young Musa ibn Maymun (Maimonides), who eventually settles in Fustat.

nodes.label: Saladin welds Egypt and Syria into one bloc
nodes.full: Sent to Egypt as a Zangid officer, Saladin made himself vizier in 1169, ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, and on Nur al-Din's death in 1174 marched on Syria. Over twelve years he took Damascus, Homs and Hama, forced Aleppo to terms in 1183 and the lord of Mosul to homage in 1186, ringing the Crusader states with a single Sunni power.
nodes.src: Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad; Lyons & Jackson (1982)

nodes.label: Saladin — the reconquest and the last years
nodes.full: Hattin in July 1187 destroyed the field army of the kingdom of Jerusalem; the holy city and most of the coast followed within the year. The Third Crusade clawed back a coastal strip, and the truce of 1192 left Saladin the interior and Jerusalem. He died at Damascus in March 1193, the realm already parcelled among some seventeen sons, brothers and nephews.

nodes.label: The war of Saladin's heirs and the rise of al-Adil
nodes.full: Saladin's sons at once fell out — al-Afdal in Damascus, al-Aziz Uthman in Cairo, al-Zahir in Aleppo — and campaigned against one another for seven years. Their uncle al-Adil played the nephews off, and by 1200 held Egypt and the senior sultanate himself.

nodes.label: Al-Adil reunites the confederation
nodes.full: A careful administrator who preferred truce and trade with the Franks to holy war, al-Adil held the confederation under his hand while parcelling its provinces among his sons: al-Kamil in Egypt, al-Mu'azzam in Damascus, al-Ashraf in the Jazira. He died in 1218 as the Fifth Crusade landed at Damietta.

nodes.label: Al-Kamil
nodes.full: Al-Kamil beat the Fifth Crusade at Mansura in 1221, ceded an unwalled Jerusalem to Frederick II by treaty in 1229, and spent twenty years at war with his brothers al-Mu'azzam and al-Ashraf for control of Syria. He briefly reunited Egypt and Damascus in 1238 and died weeks later.

nodes.label: Al-Salih Ayyub and rule by mamluk
nodes.full: Al-Salih Ayyub seized Egypt from his brother in 1240 and ruled by fear, leaning on a regiment of purchased Qipchaq Turks — the Bahriyya — and on stateless Khwarazmian horsemen who sacked Jerusalem for him in 1244. He recovered Damascus in 1245 and died at Mansura in November 1249 as Louis IX invaded.

nodes.label: Turanshah, Shajar al-Durr and the Mamluk seizure
nodes.full: Al-Salih's widow Shajar al-Durr concealed his death to hold the front against Louis IX. His son Turanshah arrived, completed the defeat of the French — then alienated the Bahriyya, who cut him down at Fariskur in May 1250. The slave-soldiers took the state; the Ayyubid line in Egypt was finished.
nodes.src: Ibn Wasil; Joinville's "Life of Saint Louis"

nodes.label: The Aleppo line
nodes.full: Al-Zahir Ghazi, Saladin's son, and then al-Aziz Muhammad ruled the rich principality of north Syria as the most autonomous Ayyubid branch — rebuilding the citadel of Aleppo, patronising scholars. The line ended when al-Nasir Yusuf, who had reunited Aleppo and Damascus, was swept away by the Mongols in 1260.

nodes.label: The Damascus line
nodes.full: Damascus passed among Saladin's and al-Adil's descendants. Al-Mu'azzam Isa (1218-1227) slighted Jerusalem's walls to deny the city to any future crusade and allied with the Khwarazm-Shah against his own kin; then came al-Ashraf, al-Salih Ismail, and finally al-Nasir Yusuf.

nodes.label: The lesser principalities — Hama, Homs, the Jazira and Yemen
nodes.full: A scatter of family holdings owed loose allegiance to whichever sultan was strongest: Hama, which survived as a Mamluk vassal until 1341; Homs and Baalbek; Mayyafariqin and Hisn Kayfa in the Jazira; and Yemen, held from Turanshah's conquest in 1174 until the Rasulids succeeded the Ayyubids there in 1229.

nodes.label: The end of the dynasty in Syria
nodes.full: With Egypt lost to the mamluks, al-Nasir Yusuf of Aleppo and Damascus was the last Ayyubid of weight. He temporised with both the Mamluks and the Mongols until Hulagu stormed Aleppo and occupied Damascus in 1260 and had him killed.

nodes.label: Hattin
nodes.full: Lured into the waterless plateau west of the Sea of Galilee, the field army of the kingdom of Jerusalem was surrounded and destroyed on 4 July 1187. Saladin captured King Guy, killed Reynald of Chatillon with his own hand, and took the relic of the True Cross.

nodes.label: The surrender of Jerusalem
nodes.full: After a short siege Balian of Ibelin negotiated terms: the Christian population was ransomed, not massacred. Saladin had the Haram al-Sharif cleansed of its Crusader additions and brought Nur al-Din's carved minbar into al-Aqsa.

nodes.label: The siege of Acre
nodes.full: The released King Guy laid siege to Acre; Saladin then besieged the besiegers, and the two armies locked around the city for two years. Philip II and Richard I broke the deadlock; when the ransom stalled, Richard had some 2,700 prisoners killed within sight of Saladin's lines.

nodes.label: Arsuf, the marches on Jerusalem and the Treaty of Jaffa
nodes.full: Richard beat Saladin at Arsuf, but twice advanced toward Jerusalem and twice turned back. The truce of September 1192 gave the Franks the coast from Tyre to Jaffa and pilgrim access to the holy places; Saladin kept the city.

nodes.label: The wars of Saladin's house
nodes.full: For seven years after Saladin's death his sons and brother fought openly for the inheritance, while the Franks, exhausted themselves, mostly watched. The fighting settled only when al-Adil had gathered Egypt, Damascus and the Jazira into his own hands.

nodes.label: Al-Kamil against his brothers
nodes.full: The confederation nearly came apart in a generation of wars among al-Kamil, al-Mu'azzam and al-Ashraf. Al-Mu'azzam allied with the Khwarazm-Shah against his own family; al-Kamil's readiness to hand Jerusalem to Frederick II in 1229 was in part a bid for a Frankish counterweight against Damascus.

nodes.label: Damietta
nodes.full: The Crusaders took Damietta after an eighteen-month siege. Al-Kamil three times offered Jerusalem and the True Cross for their withdrawal; the papal legate refused each time. The army marched on Cairo, was trapped at Mansura, and surrendered Damietta to leave.

nodes.label: The 1229 cession of Jerusalem and the Muslim reaction
nodes.full: By the Treaty of Jaffa al-Kamil handed Frederick II the city of Jerusalem — unwalled, with the Haram left in Muslim hands — for a ten-year truce. Preachers denounced the deal from the pulpits of Damascus and Cairo, and the Damascus Ayyubids repudiated it.

nodes.label: The Khwarazmian sack of Jerusalem and La Forbie
nodes.full: Al-Salih Ayyub hired the stateless Khwarazmian cavalry; in 1244 they stormed Jerusalem, wrecked the Holy Sepulchre and drove out the Christians. Weeks later the joint Egyptian and Khwarazmian army annihilated the allied Frankish and Damascene host at La Forbie.

nodes.label: Louis IX at Damietta and Mansura
nodes.full: Louis IX took an undefended Damietta in June 1249. Al-Salih Ayyub died as the French pushed inland; at Mansura the army was blockaded, starved and forced to surrender. Louis was ransomed for Damietta and 400,000 livres.

nodes.label: Köse Dagh, the tributary Jazira and the fall of Syria
nodes.full: The Mongols crushed the Seljuks of Rum at Köse Dagh in 1243, removing the buffer to the north. In 1260 Hulagu took Aleppo by storm and occupied Damascus, ending Ayyubid rule in Syria. The Mamluk victory at Ayn Jalut that year halted the advance but did not bring the dynasty back.

nodes.label: The Sunni restoration of Egypt in law
nodes.full: Saladin abolished the Ismaili courts and the Shi'i call to prayer, restored Sunni qadis of all four schools, endowed the first Sunni madrasas in Cairo and Fustat, and returned the Friday prayer to the Abbasid caliph's name — the state religion of Egypt changed from the top in under a decade.

nodes.label: The confederation as a form of government
nodes.full: The Ayyubid realm was held as family property: divided among the adult males, each a near-sovereign in his own city, owing the senior sultan military aid. Under a strong figure it worked; otherwise it tipped into civil war — the structural weakness the Mamluks replaced with a unitary state.

nodes.label: The iqta and the cadastral survey
nodes.full: The Ayyubids took over and tightened the Fatimid military iqta: an officer held the tax revenue of assigned villages for a fixed number of horsemen. Al-Kamil had Egypt re-surveyed (the rawk) around 1218.

nodes.label: Ayyubid coinage and the last figural dirhams
nodes.full: The gold dinar was debased as West African gold flowed toward the Almohads; the silver dirham became the real money of account. The Jaziran Ayyubid and Artuqid mints kept striking large figural copper coins — the last sustained tradition of images on Islamic coins.

nodes.label: The dhimma under the Ayyubids
nodes.full: Christians and Jews stayed in the fiscal bureaucracy and dominated medicine, but the Ayyubids ran a harder line than the Fatimids: the non-Muslim vizier disappears, dress rules and dismissals were enforced in waves through the 1240s and 1250s.

nodes.label: The re-Islamisation of Jerusalem
nodes.full: After 1187 Saladin reversed 88 years of Frankish Christian Jerusalem: the Templar and Hospitaller additions to the Haram were removed, al-Aqsa and the Dome of the Rock reconsecrated, and Jews permitted to resettle the city for the first time since 1099.

nodes.label: The Sunni triumph in Egypt
nodes.full: After 260 years of Ismaili rule Egypt returned to the Sunni fold with almost no friction, because the Fatimid da'wa had never converted the population. The Ayyubids planted Shafi'i and Maliki madrasas and pushed the Ismaili organisation underground or out to Yemen.

nodes.label: The four-madhhab madrasa and Ash'ari theology
nodes.full: The Ayyubid madrasa taught the four Sunni law schools with Ash'ari theology and al-Ghazali's synthesis as the norm. Al-Salih Ayyub's Salihiyya of 1242 was the first foundation in Egypt to endow chairs in all four schools at once.

nodes.label: Sufism becomes an institution of state
nodes.full: In 1173 Saladin endowed the khanqah of Sa'id al-Su'ada in Cairo — the first state-funded Sufi lodge in Egypt. His successors multiplied khanqahs across Egypt and Syria; organised, endowed Sufism moved from the margins to the centre of religious life.

nodes.label: Ibn Arabi and the unity of being, in Damascus
nodes.full: The Andalusi mystic Ibn Arabi spent his last seventeen years under Ayyubid protection in Damascus, completing the 'Meccan Openings' and writing the 'Bezels of Wisdom'. The doctrine later called wahdat al-wujud became the common idiom of later Islamic mysticism.

nodes.label: Maimonides, head of the Jews of Egypt
nodes.full: A refugee from Almohad persecution in the west, Musa ibn Maymun settled in Fustat, served as physician to Saladin's vizier and household, and was recognised as head of the Jews. Here he completed the 'Mishneh Torah' and wrote the 'Guide of the Perplexed'.

nodes.label: The Coptic golden age of Arabic letters
nodes.full: Even as the community shrank under fiscal pressure, Coptic scholarship in Arabic reached its height: the three Awlad al-Assal brothers compiled the standard Coptic canon law, a critical edition of the Arabic Gospels and Coptic-Arabic lexica.

nodes.label: The Hanbali migration to Salihiyya
nodes.full: A community of Hanbali scholars from the hills near Nablus, displaced by Frankish pressure, took root in the Salihiyya suburb of Damascus under Ayyubid patronage. Ibn Qudama's 'al-Mughni' became the great Hanbali law manual; the school that later produced Ibn Taymiyya grew from this settlement.

nodes.label: The Citadel of Cairo
nodes.full: Saladin began the fortress on the Muqattam spur to bring Cairo and Fustat under one wall; al-Kamil finished it and made it the seat of government. The Citadel was the residence of every ruler of Egypt from the 13th century until 1874.

nodes.label: The tomb-madrasa arrives in Egypt
nodes.full: The cruciform four-iwan madrasa came to Egypt from Syria and Iraq. Al-Salih Ayyub's Salihiyya of 1242, and the domed tomb his widow built for him beside it in 1250 — the first royal mausoleum on a Cairo street — began the avenue of tomb-madrasas the Mamluks would fill for 250 years.

nodes.label: The citadels of Syria and the ablaq facade
nodes.full: Al-Zahir Ghazi's rebuilding of the citadel of Aleppo is among the finest fortresses of the medieval world. The Ayyubids developed the striped light-and-dark stone courses (ablaq) and the honeycomb muqarnas portal that became the signature of Mamluk architecture.

nodes.label: Inlaid brass and the scattering of Mosul
nodes.full: Ayyubid Syria and the Jazira produced silver- and gold-inlaid brass of exceptional refinement, some carrying Christian Gospel scenes made for Muslim or Christian buyers. Metalworkers trained in Mosul dispersed into the Ayyubid cities as the Mongols closed in.

nodes.label: Enamelled glass and Raqqa ware
nodes.full: The Syrian glasshouses brought gilded and enamelled glass to maturity under the Ayyubids — the mosque lamps and beakers medieval Europe prized and imitated — while the kilns of Raqqa and Damascus turned out lustre and underglaze-painted pottery.

nodes.label: The poets of the Ayyubid courts
nodes.full: Baha al-Din Zuhayr served al-Salih Ayyub as court poet and chancery head; Ibn Sana al-Mulk revived the Andalusi muwashshah form in Egypt; and the chancery prose of al-Qadi al-Fadil, Saladin's secretary, was studied as a model for centuries.

nodes.label: Maimonides and the Guide of the Perplexed
nodes.full: Written in Judaeo-Arabic, the 'Guide of the Perplexed' set out to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with the Torah; through its Hebrew and Latin translations it shaped Jewish, Christian and some Muslim thought for centuries.

nodes.label: Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi — observation against authority
nodes.full: The Baghdad polymath taught at Saladin's Jerusalem and then Cairo, Damascus and Aleppo. His book on Egypt describes the great famine of 1200-1202 at first hand and corrects Galen on the anatomy of the jaw and sacrum by direct inspection.

nodes.label: Al-Suhrawardi and the philosophy of illumination
nodes.full: Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi built the ishraqi, illuminationist system, recasting Avicennan philosophy around a hierarchy of lights. He was put to death at Aleppo in 1191 on Saladin's order, at the urging of the city's jurists and his own son al-Zahir.

nodes.label: The historians of Saladin and the Ayyubids
nodes.full: The age produced an unusually rich and openly competing set of histories: Ibn Shaddad, Saladin's own qadi; Imad al-Din, his secretary; the Mosuli Ibn al-Athir, cool toward Saladin out of Zangid loyalty; Abu Shama; and Ibn Wasil.

nodes.label: Yaqut al-Hamawi and the encyclopedists
nodes.full: A manumitted slave of Greek origin, Yaqut compiled the 'Mu'jam al-Buldan', a vast alphabetical geography, working in Aleppo and Mosul after fleeing the first Mongol wave from Merv.

nodes.label: Ayyubid medicine and the teaching hospital
nodes.full: The Nuri hospital of Damascus became under the Ayyubids the leading medical school of the Near East. Ibn al-Nafis, who would describe the pulmonary transit of blood, trained at the Nuri before moving to Cairo.

nodes.label: The Red Sea route and the Karimi merchants
nodes.full: The Ayyubids taxed and protected the spice trade running from the Indian Ocean through Aden, up the Red Sea to Aydhab, and down the Nile to Cairo. The Karimi emerge in this period as the wealthiest merchants of the Islamic world.

nodes.label: The treaties with the Italian republics
nodes.full: Al-Adil and al-Kamil granted Venice, Pisa and Genoa fixed tariffs, resident consuls and walled trading compounds in Alexandria. Egypt supplied alum, sugar and pepper against silver, timber and iron.

nodes.label: The great famine of 1200-1202
nodes.full: A failed Nile flood followed by epidemic disease killed a large share of Egypt's population. Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi, in Cairo through it, recorded emptied villages, a collapsed food supply and, in the worst of it, cannibalism.

nodes.label: Sugar
nodes.full: Egypt and the Jordan valley were the Mediterranean's main sugar producers. Ayyubid mills pressed and boiled cane for refining and export to Europe. The crop was capital-intensive and tied closely to the state and military elite.

nodes.label: The militarised land and the shrinking of cash
nodes.full: The spread of the iqta, the army's direct claim on rural revenue, and the 13th-century shortage of good gold coin pushed the Ayyubid economy toward payment in kind rather than cash — the pattern the Mamluk state would carry to its extreme.

nodes.label: Yemen, Aden and the India trade
nodes.full: Turanshah's conquest of Yemen in 1174 gave the Ayyubids the customs house of Aden, the pivot where the Indian and Egyptian trades met. Even after the Rasulids succeeded the Ayyubids in Yemen in 1229, the Egypt-Aden-India axis defined Red Sea commerce.

nodes.label: The answer to the Crusader castle
nodes.full: Ayyubid military engineering absorbed and countered Frankish fortification: the bent entrance passage, continuous machicolation, sloping talus and concentric enceinte mature in the citadels of Ajlun, Aleppo, Bosra and Cairo.

nodes.label: Al-Jazari's Book of Ingenious Devices
nodes.full: At the Artuqid court of Amid — an Ayyubid neighbour and sometime vassal in the Jazira — al-Jazari completed his illustrated treatise describing the crankshaft, the segmental gear, and reprogrammable water-clocks and automata.

nodes.label: Anatomy from the famine dead
nodes.full: Examining the bones of the tens of thousands who died in the Egyptian famine, Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi established by direct inspection that the human lower jaw is a single bone and the sacrum normally a single fused mass — correcting Galen.

nodes.label: Water for the Citadel and the Ghouta
nodes.full: The Ayyubids built the aqueduct carrying Nile water up to the Cairo Citadel and maintained the canal and qanat network of the Ghouta oasis that made Damascus habitable — keeping a fortress-city watered under siege was itself a strategic technology.

nodes.label: The Frankish-Ayyubid truce system
nodes.full: The Ayyubids institutionalised coexistence with the Frankish coast: multi-year truces renewed almost as routine, villages whose revenue was split between the two sides, and safe-conducts for pilgrims and caravans.

nodes.label: Al-Kamil and Frederick II
nodes.full: Years of correspondence, an exchange of gifts including an astronomical tent, and finally the 1229 treaty that returned Jerusalem without a battle. The regard between the sultan and the excommunicate emperor scandalised the clergy of both faiths.

nodes.label: Usama ibn Munqidh and life across the frontier
nodes.full: The 'Book of Contemplation', the memoir of a Syrian gentleman-warrior who hunted, negotiated, doctored and dined with Franks as readily as he fought them, is the fullest first-hand Muslim picture of the Crusader Levant as a lived-in mixed society.

nodes.label: The scholars fleeing the Mongols
nodes.full: The destruction of Khwarazm, and then of Baghdad in 1258, drove astronomers, physicians, metalworkers and jurists westward into Ayyubid Syria and Egypt, which became the refuge and archive of the eastern Islamic learned tradition.

nodes.label: The Mongol ultimatum
nodes.full: Mongol envoys demanded the submission of the Jaziran and Syrian Ayyubid princes. Some sent tribute, some resisted, and al-Nasir Yusuf tried to negotiate a middle course.

nodes.label: Saladin becomes a European legend
nodes.full: Within a lifetime Western writers had turned Saladin into a model of chivalry — Old French romance, Boccaccio's Decameron, Dante placing him among the virtuous non-Christians. A Muslim enemy was absorbed into Christendom's own ideal of the noble ruler.

nodes.label: Egypt and Syria under one hand
nodes.full: For the first time since the 10th century a single Sunni authority spanned Egypt, Muslim Syria and the Jazira, aligned with the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad — the strategic encirclement of the Crusader states that made Hattin possible.

nodes.label: Outremer reduced to a coast
nodes.full: The Third Crusade recovered a coastal strip but never the interior. For the next century the Frankish Levant was a chain of fortified port cities living on trade and truces — a settlement the Ayyubids on the whole preferred to maintain rather than eliminate.

nodes.label: Egypt is the key to the Levant
nodes.full: The Fifth Crusade and the Seventh Crusade both struck at Egypt, not Jerusalem, on the recognition that whoever held the Nile could not be dislodged from Syria. Both broke at Mansura. The second brought down the dynasty that had beaten the first.

nodes.label: The Mongol shadow
nodes.full: Chinggis Khan's destruction of the Khwarazmian empire in 1219-21 sent the shock west: the stateless Khwarazmian cavalry became a wrecking force for hire, and the Mongols themselves reached the Ayyubid world through the Seljuk collapse at Köse Dagh in 1243.

nodes.label: The Mamluks take Egypt
nodes.full: The Bahriyya regiment's murder of Turanshah put a self-perpetuating corps of freed slave-soldiers in charge of the richest state in the region. Within a decade they had stopped the Mongols at Ayn Jalut and absorbed Ayyubid Syria.

nodes.label: Egypt bound into the Mediterranean economy
nodes.full: The Italian treaties, the alum, sugar and spice trades and the funduq system tied Ayyubid Egypt structurally to Venice, Pisa and Genoa. The commercial relationship outlived the dynasty by three centuries.

nodes.label: Shajar al-Durr
nodes.full: The Turkic slave-concubine of al-Salih Ayyub concealed his death to keep the army together against Louis IX, then in 1250 was proclaimed sultana of Egypt in her own name — the only woman to rule medieval Egypt outright. She married the Mamluk Aybak, had him killed in 1257, and was beaten to death days later.

nodes.label: The princess-builders of Ayyubid Syria
nodes.full: Dayfa Khatun, granddaughter of Saladin's brother, governed Aleppo as regent from 1236 to 1242 and founded two great khanqahs. Other Ayyubid women endowed madrasas and tomb-complexes across Damascus — the religious endowment was the channel of durable public agency for elite women.

nodes.label: The mamluk regiments before the coup
nodes.full: The Bahriyya — al-Salih Ayyub's regiment of purchased Qipchaq Turks, quartered on Rawda island — together with the earlier Salihiyya and Asadiyya corps: slave households that developed a corporate identity and a political will years before they seized the state in 1250.

nodes.label: The Coptic community under pressure
nodes.full: The Ayyubid century brought episodic dress edicts, dismissals of Coptic officials, and a wave of pressure in the 1250s — even as Copto-Arabic scholarship reached its height. The long demographic decline of Egyptian Christianity is usually dated from about here.

nodes.label: The beloved youth in Ayyubid letters
nodes.full: The poetry and adab of the Ayyubid courts carry on the long convention of the love lyric addressed to a beautiful youth, alongside the jurists' flat condemnation of the act itself — the distance between literary sensibility and the letter of the law.

nodes.label: The slave supply of Egypt
nodes.full: Enslaved people reached Egypt down the Nile from Nubia, across the Red Sea, across the Mediterranean, and increasingly across the Black Sea from the Qipchaq steppe — the last stream furnishing the Turkish military slaves who would become the folio's own successor ruling class.
